the cause, measured, and how I fix it

You asked to see the wording, so the AFTER picture is the wording.

First, what the arrow actually does — I read the code rather than guessing, because it decides how the message should read. Outdenting moves the item up one level and takes everything inside it along. Nothing is deleted, and the → arrow puts it back. So the dialog must not look like a danger warning — a red "are you sure?" for a reversible move trains you to click through every dialog, including the ones that matter.

What the wording does:
• asks a plain question in the title — "Move this out to its own branch?"
• names the item and its parent, so you know which row you hit
• shows the move as now → after, rather than describing it
• says what travels with it — anything inside moves too
• says it is reversible, naming the → that undoes it
• the confirm button says Move it out, not "OK" — the button names the action, so it reads correctly if you skim.

The picture shows: the exact wording for you to read and change.

And a second fault underneath it, which is why your second sentence matters. You said "same thing in the priority tree section". Measured: every row has two outdent arrows — .tree-outdent in the row controls and .rowquick.q-out — and the confirm was wired to window.__outdentNode. But that function is defined as "find the row and click .tree-outdent", so pressing the arrow you can actually see goes straight to the real handler and skips the dialog entirely. So the fix is two things, not one: put the wording back, and hook it at the place the work actually happens rather than at a wrapper that the real button walks past. I will prove it by pressing both arrows with a real pointer.

the cause, measured, and how I fix it

REPRODUCED — and the setting is never touched
I left Show future branches OFF for the whole test and only pressed › on the tree date. Future items appear anyway.
Measured, counting the future rows on screen at each step:
tree datesettingfuture rows showingshould be
TodayOFF00 ✓
+1 dayOFF10
+3 daysOFF20
The cause, in one line of the app’s own code:
var today = (window.selectedDate || todayISO());  // the TREE DATE, not the clock
var realToday = todayISO();  // computed right here, and NOT used for this
var isFuture = !!(date && date > today);
"Future" is measured against the date at the top of the tree. Step that date forward and yesterday’s future becomes today’s present, so the rows unhide — while the switch you actually set sits there doing nothing. realToday is already sitting on the line above, used only for "overdue".

I FIXED THIS THE WRONG WAY FIRST — corrected 2026-10-30
I measured "future" from the real clock. That stopped the leak and broke something you rely on: an item never became due no matter how far forward you read. You found it in one move.
Measured on three items due in 1, 6 and 20 days, tree date moved to +6:
ruledue in 1due in 6due in 20
tree date (original, and now)shownshownhidden ✓
clock (my first fix)hiddenhiddenhidden
The rule, as you describe it: moving the tree date forward is reading that day. Anything due by then is present and must appear; only what is still beyond it is "future". That line is back as it was.

So what was actually broken? Not this rule — the gear switch, which is the rest of this card. It could not be turned on, so there was never a way to deliberately look further ahead than the day you were reading. That half of the fix stands and is in the demo.

AND A SECOND FAULT, found because you asked for the "setting ON" picture
I could not take that picture — the switch will not turn on at all. I pressed it, read the setting back, and it was still off.
I trapped every write to the setting and watched who moved it:
hideFuture → false  by toggleHideFuture — your press
hideFuture → true  by settings() — immediately after
hideFuture → true  by settings() — and again on every render
A helper that runs on every render carries the line s.hideFuture = true; — not as a default, but as an order. So the switch flips for a fraction of a second and is overwritten before anything is drawn. It has never been able to stay on.

Proven: I changed that one line to set a default instead of forcing a value (if (typeof s.hideFuture !== 'boolean')) and the switch worked at once — setting went off, two future rows appeared, and it survived a redraw.

So card 2 is two faults in one place: the tree date leaks future items in when the switch is off, and the switch cannot be turned on to ask for them deliberately. Fixing only the first would leave you with no way to see ahead at all.

The picture shows: the priority tree with the tree date on today, the gear switch pressed in both.

I also thought of — you have not decided this yet

What I checked before writing this, so we do not go back and forth:

  • The setting really was off. I read __revealAhead at every step — false throughout. This is not the switch misbehaving.
  • It is not about my test data. With the tree date left on today the rows hide correctly, so the rule itself works; only moving the date breaks it.
  • I drove the real control, the › beside the tree date, not a variable. Setting selectedDate by hand does not re-render, which would have hidden the fault.
One thing worth your word before I build it. Card 48, which is already live, deliberately makes the tree date drive the missed-routine rule — move the date forward and yesterday counts as missed. This card moves the future rule the other way, back onto the clock. I think that is right: "what have I missed" follows the day you are reading, while "do not show me things that have not happened yet" should follow real time, or the switch means nothing. But they are two rules pulling in opposite directions, and you should be the one to say so.

You were right to ask for the ON picture. I had drawn this card without it, and it would have shipped a fix to one fault while the switch stayed dead — you would have pressed it, seen nothing, and been back here. The missing picture was the missing test.

A THIRD FAULT, found while building this
Before publishing I pressed the real gear menu item instead of calling the function my own check had been calling. It did nothing.
There are two separate switches behind one control. The gear item calls __futToggle, which writes its own flag and draws the tick and the count. But the rows are hidden by a different mechanism that watches __revealAhead, owned by a different function. So the button flipped a flag nothing was watching — and the menu was even showing the count "1" for a branch it then refused to reveal.

The third fix: the button keeps its own state, and now carries the other along with it, so one press means one thing.

What this would have cost you: shipping the first two fixes alone would have stopped the leak and left you with no way to see ahead at all — the switch would still have been dead. My check had been calling the function, so it would have passed. A check that calls the function tests the function; only pressing the button tests the button. It now presses the button.

MY RECOMMENDATION
Build it as pictured, with two changes I would argue for:

1. Let Missed combine rather than override. In the tree it answers "what has slipped across my whole planner", so overriding is right there. Inside one task the list is already short, and "the overdue ones AND the ones coming up" is a reasonable thing to want.

2. Drop "Show routines & habits" unless you actually put routines inside a task. It earns its place in the tree because routines live there; on this fixture it does nothing. I have pictured it so you can judge, but I would leave it out and keep the menu to four working lines.
Two more to settle:
  • One setting for all items, or per item? I would say one for all, like the tree — otherwise the same window opens differently depending on which task you came from.
  • Do the switches survive closing the window? The tree’s stay on until you turn them off; I would match that.
On the colour, and what I got wrong. I decoded your screenshot and measured rgb(96,65,35) — that part was right. What I got wrong was the conclusion: I treated a deliberate design choice as a defect and brightened it. The tree’s own comment beside that rule reads "the future date — metadata, never competing with the task". Measuring a value is not the same as knowing whether it is wrong, and you were the one who knew.
